latin.159: CAP. II. Status Questionis. Venio nunc ad statum questionis. Eum non incommode constituisses si poenae nomini, quod in eam introduxisti, ambiguitatem vel non inclusisses, vel sustulisses. Enimvero poenae nomine corruptionem haereditariam complecti vel voluisti, vel noluisti. Si noluisti: debuisti id significare, alioqui erraturo lectori, quippe cum hoc primo capite innuas, et secundo clames, et aliis inculces, corruptionem illam poenam esse primi peccati. Si voluisti, vel putasti corruptionem illam esse poenam proprie dictam primi peccati, non solum quatenus in ipso Adamo fuit, sed etiam quatenus inest in nobis; vel non. Si prius, quaestionem non admitto: Praesupponit enim ut certum, ut inter nos confessum, id quod ego thesibus meis refutavi, quodque versatur in quaestione, nimirum corruptionem haereditariam esse, proprie et stricte loquendo, poenam primi peccati, non solum quatenus fuit in Adamo sed etiam quatenus nobis propagata inest. Si poenam quidem esse voluisti, sed non proprie dictam, nec stricta hujus vocabuli significatione, saltem quatenus est in nobis, decuit te mentem tuam explicare, quoniam apparet ex multis hujus tui tractatus locis te corruptionem illam putare poenam esse sensu strictissimo, maximeque proprio.
latin.160: Misso igitur poenae nomine, potuisses sic quaestionem instituisse sine ulla ambiguitate: Cur nascamur obnoxii miseriis hujus vitae, morti corporis, et morti aeternae? an quia nobis imputetur proxime et immediate primum peccatum actuale Adami? aut quia sine ejusmodi imputatione, vitiositas ejus ab eo in nos derivata est, et per propagationem naturalem transfusa? Tu prius affirmas, ego posterius. Vel sic, Cur trahimus ab Adamo corruptionem moralem haereditariam, quae peccatum originale dici solet? An quia nobis a Deo Judice primum peccatum actuale Adami imputetur, ac in ejus imputati poenam, ut vindicetur, et justitiae satisfiat, infligatur illa corruptio moralis, quae et ipsa peccatum est, et fons aliorum peccatorum? Aut vero quia, sine ejusmodi imputatione, haec est naturae lex ante peccatum constituta, ut sui quaeque res similem gignat, homo hominem, corruptus corruptum, vitiosus vitiosum, leprosus leprosum? Tu rursus prius asseris, ego posterius. Quamvis autem status questionis, ita propositus accommodate ad mentem tuam, non prorsus incommodus sit, nondum tamen mihi omni ex parte satisfacit: exprimit enim potius partes questionis, quam ipsam quaestionem universam.
latin.161: Ut igitur, quando de mea sententia agitur, quid sentiam distincte aperiam, atque statum questionis, quoad ejus fieri a me poterit, dilucide et enucleate constituam, eam dividam in duas, quarum altera est de imputatione primi peccati Adami, altera de poena, qua imputatum vindicari dicitur. Quaeritur enim primum, Utrum primum peccatum Adami omnibus ejus posteris, Christo excepto, imputetur? Deinde, Utrum corruptio haereditaria nobis infligatur a Deo Judice, ut fiat justitia? Priori quaestioni, quia laborat homonymia, non possum per simplicem affirmationem, aut negationem respondere. Distinguendum enim ejus est tum subjectum, tum attributum. Subjectum est primum peccatum Adami: in quo duo distinguenda, Actio tam interna quam externa, qua divinum interdictum violavit, et Corruptio moralis, quam illa actio in Adami naturam intulit. Quae corruptio ipsa quoque spectari potest duobus modis, uno ut fuit in Adamo; altero, ut est in nobis profecta ab Adamo. Hinc fit ut primum peccatum Adami usurpetur quatuor modis.
latin.162: 1. pro actione qua dei legem est transgressus, quae primum fuit peccatum actuale. 2. pro eadem illa actione non praecise accepta, sed simul cum habituali corruptione quam peperit: habent enim se haec duo velut calefactio et calor, actus et habitus, mutatio actualis et mutatio habitualis. Itaque utrumque conjunctim idem nomen peccati Adami, vel primi peccati nonnunquam complectitur. 3. pro corruptione, quam actualis inobedientia genuit in Adamo, quaeque fuit ejus primum peccatum habituale. 4. denique pro eadem illa corruptione in nos transmissa et propagata, quae nostrum quidem peccatum est, quia nobis inhaeret, nos afficit, et denominat; dicitur tamen peccatum Adami ut authoris, ut primi veluti possessoris, ut fontis unde ad nos defluxit. Si hoc ultimo modo sumatur primum Adami peccatum, aio illud omnibus Adami posteris (uno, in quo locum nullum habuit, Christo excepto) imputari, donec ab eo per Christum justificentur, eorumque sententiam jure damnatam a Synodo Carentonensi arbitror, qui hoc quidem peccatum agnoscere se profitentur, nulli tamen imputari, quantumvis infideli: esse enim hoc saeculo qui id doceant editis libris testatur et deplorat paulo ante obitum suum in quadam Epistola doctissimus Walaeus. Similiter si tertio modo sumatur, fateor nobis imputari, non tamen qua haesit in Adamo, sed qua in nos transit, ac, ut verbis utar Calvini, quia intra nos est: est enim nostra corruptio haereditaria eadem specie cum illa, quae olim fuit in Adamo; ac quam suam naturam, tam suam corruptionem moralem nobiscum Adamus communicavit.
latin.163: Idem de secundo modo dicendum: quam enim vere dicitur peccatum Adami in nos transiisse, derivatum, transmissum, propagatum esse, tam vere etiam dicitur nobis imputari. Propagatum est autem, non qua fuit actio transiens, sed qua fuit vitiositas permanens, non qua fuit peccatum personae, sed qua fuit peccatum naturae, non qua olim esse desiit in rerum natura, sed qua naturae humanae adhaeret, cumque ea multiplicatur et propagatur. Porro ut natura mea propagata et derivata ab Adamo differt numero a natura Adami, sic peccatum ab Adamo derivatum et propagatum differt numero a peccato Adami. Hactenus, nisi me fallit animus, inter nos summus est consensus, modo nolis negare corruptionem haereditariam esse vere peccatum irregenitis imputabile, vel potius imputandum ad condemnationem. Quod si id neges, haec tertia exorietur inter me et te controversia, qua quamvis propriis argumentis confici poterit, tamen iis nihil opus erit: nam refutatis (quod feci in Thesibus) exceptionibus Socini, Pelagii, et Pighii, necesse est fateri, universam illam condemnationem, quam Apostolus ad Rom. v.12. inculcat, ex sola illa corruptione, quae a lapsu Adami fluxit, proxime enasci. PLAC. Has tres ultimas peccati Adamici acceptiones D. Gar. mirum in modum exagitat: qua mente? nescio. Nihil enim id juvat statum questionis, aut causam quam agit, et Lectorem inutiliter moratur. Quid enim in ea nominis distinctione reprehendit? Num eam falsitatis arguit? minime. Num negat in ea re consensum esse? nequaquam. Quid ergo agit? ipsum audi.
latin.164: GAR. Primum quidem est, quod suam praestanti Theologo confessionem gratuemur, qui, etsi negat imputari posteris primam illam Adae actionem, qua Dei mandatum violavit, si eam praecise ac seorsim spectemus; agnoscit tamen illam imputari, acceptam simul cum corruptione quam peperit. Hoc enim inde certo consequitur, ergo ipsam criminosam Adami actionem posteris imputari: quoniam quod simul et conjunctim cum alio spectatum imputatur, non eo tantum minus imputari censendum est. Jam vero si Adami actio, non praecise sumpta, sed simul cum corruptione consequenti, imputatur; nemo non videt, eas omnes rationes una veluti litura expungendas, quibus adversus actionis Adamicae imputationem hactenus Viri Docti disputarunt. Illae enim omnes id efficiunt, si quid efficiunt, nos nullo modo esse posse reos propter inobedientiam et actionem injustam alterius nobis imputatam, sive praecise, sive una cum alio vel actu, vel habitu illam considerare libeat. Illud autem si fixum maneat, actionem Adami simul cum corruptione, quam peperit, acceptam unicuique posterorum imputari, pax facile componetur. PLAC. In elogio praestantis theologi, quo me ornat indignum, judicium charitatis agnosco. In reliquis ejus verbis quatuor mihi apparent ὀράματα. Primum enim sententiam mihi tribuit, quae mea non est. Nunquam enim negavi ipsam criminosam actionem Adami posteris ejus imputari. Nunquam affirmavi nos nullo modo esse posse reos propter inobedientiam Adami. Tantummodo negavi illam actionem posteris imputari immediate, et nos esse reos propter illam immediate. Nam illam imputari mediate, propter illam nos esse reos mediate, id est, mediante corruptione ab illa in nos descendente, ego toties dixi, repetiui, inculcavi, ut mirum sit virum doctum ad has meas voces toties iteratas obsurduisse.
latin.165: Deinde, non modo perdit operam in eo contra me probando quod passim affirmo, sed, quod deterius est, id inde elicere conatur, ubi non latet. Etsi enim verba mea prima fronte favere videantur ejus collectioni, tamen ei praescindit omnem ansam, quae continuo sequitur explicatio, quam ipse libri sui pag. 33. sic contraxerat, quia, quam vere peccatum Adami in nos transit, tam vere nobis imputari dicitur. Atqui transit et propagatum est, non qua fuit actio transiens, sed qua fuit vitiositas permanens, nec qua fuit peccatum personae, sed qua fuit peccatum naturae, quod scilicet naturae humanae adhaeret, et cum ea multiplicatur atque propagatur. Tertio, falsum est nostras omnes rationes, si quid efficiunt, efficere nos nullo modo esse reos propter inobedientiam Adami: Eas enim imputationem illius inobedientiae mediatam nullo modo impugnare tam clare ostendi datis ad eum literis, ut ab eo responsionem nulla etiam agitatione impetrare potuerim. Quarto denique falsum est id quod ait, si fixum maneat actionem Adami simul cum corruptione quam peperit acceptam unicuique posterorum imputari, pacem facile compositum iri. Restabit enim integra quaestio, utrum illa actio praecise sumpta immediate imputetur, hoc est, ita, ut illius imputatae corruptio sit poena proprie dicta. Id quod unum duntaxat et constanter negavi, et negatum volui. Praecisam enim a corruptione, quae in Adamo et nobis haesit, imputari oportet, si quidem illam imputationem corruptio sequitur ut poena.

pass_a.159: CHAPTER II. Status of the question. I come now to the status of the question. You would not have set it awkwardly if to the name of penalty, which you introduced into it, you had either not included ambiguity, or had removed it. For truly, by the name of penalty you either wished to embrace hereditary corruption, or you did not wish to. If you did not wish to: you ought to have signified that, otherwise to the reader about to err, inasmuch as in this first chapter you hint, and in the second you cry out, and to others you inculcate, that that corruption is the penalty of the first sin. If you wished, or thought, that that corruption is the penalty properly so called of the first sin, not only inasmuch as it was in Adam himself, but also inasmuch as it is in us; or not. If the former, I do not admit the question: For it presupposes as certain, as confessed among us, that which I refuted by my theses, and which is at issue in the question, namely that hereditary corruption is, properly and strictly speaking, the penalty of the first sin, not only inasmuch as it was in Adam but also inasmuch as it is present propagated to us. If indeed you wished it to be a penalty, but not properly so called, nor in the strict signification of this word, at least inasmuch as it is in us, it was fitting that you explain your mind, since it appears from many places of this your treatise that you think that corruption to be a penalty in the strictest sense, and most properly.
pass_a.160: Therefore with the name of penalty set aside, you could have instituted the question thus without any ambiguity: Why are we born liable to the miseries of this life, to the death of the body, and to eternal death? is it because the first actual sin of Adam is imputed to us proximately and immediately? or because without such imputation, his viciousness has been derived from him into us, and transfused by natural propagation? You affirm the former, I the latter. Or thus: Why do we draw from Adam hereditary moral corruption, which is wont to be called original sin? Is it because by God the Judge the first actual sin of Adam is imputed to us, and for the penalty of that imputed sin, that it may be vindicated, and justice satisfied, that moral corruption is inflicted which is itself also sin, and the fountain of other sins? Or truly because, without such imputation, this is the law of nature constituted before the sin, that each thing generate its like, man a man, the corrupt the corrupt, the vicious the vicious, the leprous the leprous? You again assert the former, I the latter. Although however the status of the question, thus proposed accommodatingly to your mind, is not utterly inconvenient, yet it does not yet satisfy me in every part: for it expresses rather the parts of the question, than the universal question itself.
pass_a.161: Therefore so that, when it is treated of my opinion, I may distinctly open what I sense, and may constitute the status of the question, as far as it will be able to be done by me, lucidly and clearly, I will divide it into two, of which one is concerning the imputation of the first sin of Adam, the other concerning the penalty by which the imputed is said to be vindicated. For it is asked first, Whether the first sin of Adam is imputed to all his posterity, Christ excepted? Then, Whether hereditary corruption is inflicted on us by God the Judge, that justice may be done? To the prior question, because it labors with homonymy, I cannot respond by a simple affirmation or negation. For both its subject and its attribute must be distinguished. The subject is the first sin of Adam: in which two things are to be distinguished, the Act both internal and external, by which he violated the divine interdict, and the moral Corruption which that act brought into Adam's nature. Which corruption itself also can be regarded in two ways, one as it was in Adam; the other, as it is in us proceeding from Adam. Hence it comes about that the first sin of Adam is used in four modes.
pass_a.162: 1. for the act by which he transgressed the law of God, which was the first actual sin. 2. for that same act not taken precisely, but together with the habitual corruption which it brought forth: for these two stand to each other as heating and heat, act and habit, actual change and habitual change. And so both jointly sometimes embrace the same name of Adam's sin, or of the first sin. 3. for the corruption which actual disobedience generated in Adam, and which was his first habitual sin. 4. finally for that same corruption transmitted and propagated into us, which indeed is our sin, because it inheres in us, affects us, and denominates us; yet it is called Adam's sin as of the author, as of the first as it were possessor, as of the fountain whence it flowed down to us. If in this last mode the first sin of Adam is taken, I affirm that it is imputed to all Adam's posterity (one excepted, in whom it had no place, Christ), until they are justified from it through Christ, and I judge their opinion rightly condemned by the Synod of Charenton, who profess that they acknowledge this sin indeed, yet that it is imputed to no one, however unbelieving: for that there are in this age who teach this in published books, the most learned Walaeus testifies and deplores a little before his death in a certain Epistle. Likewise if it is taken in the third mode, I confess it is imputed to us, yet not as it stuck in Adam, but as it passes into us, and, to use Calvin's words, because it is within us: for our hereditary corruption is the same in species with that which once was in Adam; and Adam communicated with us as much his nature as his moral corruption.
pass_a.163: The same must be said of the second mode: for as truly as Adam's sin is said to have passed into us, to have been derived, transmitted, propagated, so truly also it is said to be imputed to us. But it has been propagated, not as it was a transient act, but as it was a permanent viciousness, not as it was the sin of a person, but as it was the sin of nature, not as it once ceased to be in the nature of things, but as it adheres to human nature, and with it is multiplied and propagated. Further, as my nature propagated and derived from Adam differs in number from Adam's nature, so the sin derived and propagated from Adam differs in number from Adam's sin. Thus far, unless my mind deceives me, there is supreme consensus between us, provided you are unwilling to deny that hereditary corruption is truly a sin imputable to the unregenerate, or rather to be imputed unto condemnation. But if you deny that, this third controversy will arise between me and you, which although it will be able to be finished by proper arguments, yet there will be no need of them: for with the exceptions of Socinus, Pelagius, and Pighius refuted (which I did in the Theses), it is necessary to confess that that universal condemnation which the Apostle inculcates at Rom. 5:12 arises proximately from that corruption alone which flowed from Adam's fall. PLAC. These three last acceptations of Adam's sin D. Gar. agitates in a marvelous manner: with what mind? I know not. For that helps nothing the status of the question, or the cause which he urges, and uselessly delays the Reader. For what does he reprehend in that distinction of the name? Does he charge it with falsity? Not at all. Does he deny that there is consensus in that matter? By no means. What then does he do? Hear him himself.
pass_a.164: GAR. First indeed it is, that we congratulate his confession to the excellent Theologian, who, although he denies that that first act of Adam, by which he violated God's command, is imputed to posterity, if we regard it precisely and separately; yet acknowledges that it is imputed, taken together with the corruption which it brought forth. For from this it certainly follows, therefore the criminal act of Adam itself is imputed to posterity: since what is imputed regarded together and jointly with another is not to be thought less imputed for that reason alone. Now indeed if Adam's act, not taken precisely, but together with the consequent corruption, is imputed; no one fails to see that all those reasons are to be expunged as with one erasure, by which Learned Men have hitherto disputed against the imputation of the Adamic act. For those all effect this, if they effect anything, that we can in no way be guilty on account of the disobedience and unjust act of another imputed to us, whether precisely, or whether it is allowed to consider it together with another either act or habit. But if that remains fixed, that Adam's act taken together with the corruption which it brought forth is imputed to each of the posterity, peace will easily be composed. PLAC. In the elogium of the excellent theologian, with which he adorns me unworthy, I acknowledge the judgment of charity. In the remaining of his words four ὀράματα appear to me. For first he attributes to me an opinion which is not mine. For I never denied that the criminal act of Adam itself is imputed to his posterity. I never affirmed that we can in no way be guilty on account of Adam's disobedience. I only denied that that act is imputed to posterity immediately, and that we are guilty on account of it immediately. For that it is imputed mediately, that we are guilty on account of it mediately, that is, by the mediating corruption descending from it into us, I have so often said, repeated, inculcated, that it is marvelous that a learned man has grown deaf to these my voices so often iterated.
pass_a.165: Then, he not only loses labor in proving against me that which I everywhere affirm, but, what is worse, he tries to elicit it from there, where it does not lie hidden. For although my words at first sight seem to favor his inference, yet every handle is cut off from him by the explanation which continuously follows, which he himself had thus contracted at page 33 of his book, because, as truly as Adam's sin passes into us, so truly it is said to be imputed to us. But it passes and has been propagated, not as it was a transient act, but as it was a permanent viciousness, nor as it was the sin of a person, but as it was the sin of nature, which namely adheres to human nature, and with it is multiplied and propagated. Third, it is false that all our reasons, if they effect anything, effect that we are in no way guilty on account of Adam's disobedience: For that they in no way impugn the mediate imputation of that disobedience I showed so clearly by letters given to him, that I could obtain a response from him by no agitation. Fourth finally it is false what he says, that if it remains fixed that Adam's act taken together with the corruption which it brought forth is imputed to each of the posterity, peace will easily be composed. For the entire question will remain, whether that act taken precisely is imputed immediately, that is, so that the corruption of that imputed act is a penalty properly so called. Which alone I have constantly denied, and wished denied. For it must be imputed precise from the corruption which stuck in Adam and in us, if indeed corruption follows that imputation as penalty.

159: Chapter II. The state of the question. I come now to the state of the question. You would not have framed it awkwardly if, in the word penalty that you brought into it, you had either left out the ambiguity or taken it away. For by penalty you either meant to include hereditary corruption, or you did not. If you did not, you should have said so—otherwise the reader will go wrong—since in this first chapter you hint, in the second you cry out, and elsewhere you drum into others, that that corruption is the penalty of the first sin. If you meant, or thought, that that corruption is the first sin's penalty in the proper sense, not only as it was in Adam himself but also as it is in us—or not—then, if the former, I refuse the question. It assumes as settled among us what I refuted in my theses and what is still under dispute: that hereditary corruption is, properly and strictly, the penalty of the first sin not only as it was in Adam but also as it is present in us by propagation. If you meant a penalty, but not properly so called, nor in the strict sense of the word—at least as it is in us—you ought to have explained your mind; for from many places in this treatise of yours it is plain that you take that corruption to be a penalty in the strictest and most proper sense.
160: So drop the word penalty, and you could have put the question without ambiguity: Why are we born liable to the miseries of this life, to bodily death, and to eternal death? Because Adam's first actual sin is imputed to us proximately and immediately? Or because, without any such imputation, his viciousness has come down from him into us and been poured through by natural propagation? You affirm the first; I the second. Or put it this way: Why do we draw from Adam that hereditary moral corruption usually called original sin? Because God the Judge imputes Adam's first actual sin to us, and, as the penalty of that imputed sin—so that it may be avenged and justice satisfied—inflicts that moral corruption which is itself sin and the spring of other sins? Or rather because, without such imputation, this was nature's law before the fall: like begets like—man a man, the corrupt the corrupt, the vicious the vicious, the leprous the leprous? Again you assert the first; I the second. Though the state of the question, framed to fit your mind, is not wholly unserviceable, it still does not satisfy me on every side: it states the parts of the question more than the question as a whole.
161: So when my own view is at stake, that I may say plainly what I hold, and set the state of the question as clearly as I can, I divide it in two: one part on the imputation of Adam's first sin, the other on the penalty by which the imputed sin is said to be avenged. First: Is Adam's first sin imputed to all his posterity, Christ excepted? Second: Is hereditary corruption inflicted on us by God the Judge so that justice may be done? To the first I cannot answer with a bare yes or no, for the wording is ambiguous. Subject and attribute must both be distinguished. The subject is Adam's first sin, in which two things are to be marked: the act, inward and outward, by which he broke the divine ban, and the moral corruption that act brought into Adam's nature. That corruption itself may be viewed two ways: as it was in Adam, and as it is in us as it came from Adam. Hence Adam's first sin is used in four senses.
162: 1. For the act by which he broke God's law—the first actual sin. 2. For that same act not taken by itself, but together with the habitual corruption it produced: the two stand as heating to heat, act to habit, actual change to habitual change. So both together sometimes share the one name 'Adam's sin' or 'the first sin.' 3. For the corruption that actual disobedience bred in Adam—his first habitual sin. 4. For that same corruption as transmitted and propagated into us, which is our sin because it inheres in us, affects us, and names us; yet it is called Adam's as of the author, the first as it were possessor, the fountain from which it flowed to us. If Adam's first sin is taken in this last sense, I say it is imputed to all Adam's posterity (Christ alone excepted, in whom it had no place) until they are justified from it through Christ; and I judge rightly condemned by the Synod of Charenton the opinion of those who profess to acknowledge this sin yet deny that it is imputed to anyone, however unbelieving—for that some in this age teach so in print, the learned Walaeus testified and mourned shortly before his death in a letter. Likewise if it is taken in the third sense, I grant that it is imputed to us—not as it clung in Adam, but as it passes into us, and, in Calvin's words, because it is within us: for our hereditary corruption is the same in kind as that which once was in Adam; and Adam shared with us his nature and his moral corruption alike.
163: The same holds for the second sense: as truly as Adam's sin is said to have passed into us—derived, transmitted, propagated—so truly it is said to be imputed to us. But it was propagated not as a passing act, but as lasting viciousness; not as the sin of a person, but as the sin of nature; not as something that once ceased to exist, but as what clings to human nature and is multiplied and propagated with it. And as my nature, derived from Adam, differs numerically from Adam's nature, so the sin derived and propagated from Adam differs numerically from Adam's sin. Thus far, unless I am mistaken, we are in full agreement—provided you will not deny that hereditary corruption is truly a sin to be imputed to the unregenerate, or rather to be imputed unto condemnation. If you deny that, a third controversy rises between us; and though it could be settled by its own arguments, they will not be needed: once Socinus's, Pelagius's, and Pighius's exceptions are answered (as I did in the Theses), we must admit that the whole condemnation Paul presses in Romans 5:12 arises proximately from that corruption alone which flowed from Adam's fall. Placeus. Master Garissoles works up these three last senses of Adam's sin strangely—to what end I do not know. It helps neither the state of the question nor the cause he urges, and only wastes the reader's time. What fault does he find in the distinction of the name? That it is false? Not at all. That there is no consensus on the point? By no means. What then is he doing? Hear him.
164: Garissoles. First we may congratulate the excellent theologian on his confession: though he denies that Adam's first act, by which he broke God's command, is imputed to posterity if we view it precisely and apart, he still grants that it is imputed when taken together with the corruption it produced. From this it surely follows that Adam's criminal act itself is imputed to posterity: for what is imputed when viewed jointly with something else is not for that reason less imputed. And if Adam's act is imputed not taken precisely but together with the following corruption, anyone can see that all the reasons learned men have used against imputing Adam's act are to be wiped out at a stroke. For if those reasons prove anything, they prove that we cannot be guilty for another's disobedience and unjust act imputed to us—whether taken alone or together with some other act or habit. But if it stands fixed that Adam's act, taken with the corruption it produced, is imputed to each of his posterity, peace will easily be made. Placeus. In the praise with which this excellent theologian honors me—unworthy as I am—I recognize charity's judgment. In the rest of his words four ὀράματα (phantasms) appear to me. First, he pins on me an opinion that is not mine. I never denied that Adam's criminal act itself is imputed to his posterity. I never said we cannot in any way be guilty for Adam's disobedience. I only denied that that act is imputed to posterity immediately, and that we are guilty for it immediately. That it is imputed mediately, and that we are guilty for it mediately—that is, through the corruption descending from it into us—I have said, repeated, and pressed so often that it is strange a learned man should have gone deaf to words so often spoken.
165: Next, he not only wastes labor proving against me what I everywhere affirm, but—worse—tries to draw it from a place where it is not hidden. My words may at first glance seem to favor his inference; yet the explanation that follows at once cuts off every handle, the explanation he himself had shortened at page 33 of his book: because, as truly as Adam's sin passes into us, so truly it is said to be imputed to us. But it passes and has been propagated not as a passing act but as lasting viciousness; not as a person's sin but as nature's sin—what clings to human nature and is multiplied and propagated with it. Third, it is false that all our reasons, if they prove anything, prove that we are in no way guilty for Adam's disobedience: for that they do not touch the mediate imputation of that disobedience I showed so clearly in letters to him that I could get no answer from him by any urging. Fourth, and last, it is false that if Adam's act, taken with the corruption it produced, remains imputed to each of the posterity, peace will be easily made. The whole question will still stand: whether that act, taken precisely, is imputed immediately—that is, so that the corruption of the imputed act is a penalty in the proper sense. That alone I have constantly denied, and wished denied. For the act must be imputed cut off from the corruption that clung in Adam and in us, if corruption is to follow that imputation as its penalty.
